FunMel

From confrontation-plate photographs to reviewed colony measurements, matched melanization coefficients and plate-aware treatment comparisons.

FunMel analyzes confrontation-plate photographs, measures target-colony image darkness and geometry, and links each treatment to the controls specified in experimental metadata. The default layout supports four approximately round Zymoseptoria tritici colonies surrounding a central fungal colony and its surrounding halo candidate. Melanization is measured on the four target Z. tritici colonies; the central fungus and halo are segmented separately and excluded from target-colony MI summaries. Layouts, dish diameter and segmentation settings can be adjusted for other supported arrangements. Colony outlines follow detected regions. Organism identities must be supplied by the experimenter.

FunMel retains the original MycoHalo function names for compatibility.

1. Install and start

Use R >= 4.1. Source installation requires a compiler: on macOS install Xcode Command Line Tools; on Windows use the Rtools version matching your R release; on Linux install an R development toolchain and the system libraries required by magick. Consult magick installation. CRAN dependencies can normally be installed as binaries on macOS/Windows.

Restart R before installing over an existing loaded version.

Install from GitHub

Install the package from GitHub with remotes:

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("mghotbi/FunMel")

The source repository is mghotbi/FunMel. The default installation uses its default branch.

To build and install the vignette locally:

install.packages(c("remotes", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))
remotes::install_github("mghotbi/FunMel",
                        build_vignettes=TRUE, dependencies=TRUE)
library(FunMel)
vignette("FunMel", package="FunMel")

Building vignettes also requires Pandoc, normally provided with RStudio. GitHub installation requires the source-compilation tools described above. Private repositories additionally require GitHub authentication. An optional ref="TAG_OR_BRANCH" selects a specific version or development branch.

Install from a source archive 

install.packages(c("cli", "magick", "Rcpp", "lme4", "lmerTest", "ggplot2"))
install.packages(file.choose(), repos=NULL, type="source")
# Choose FunMel_0.3.7.tar.gz. Restart R again after installation.
library(FunMel)
packageVersion("FunMel")                 # installed version: 0.3.7
getNamespaceVersion("FunMel")            # loaded version: also 0.3.7
vignette("FunMel", package="FunMel")
help(package="FunMel")

With a custom library, pass the same lib to installation and lib.loc to library(). If the installed and loaded versions differ, restart R; loading again does not replace an already loaded namespace.

2. Explore the bundled 14-day case study

The bundled case study contains measured data from 20 photographs in five matched sets. Each set has one control plate and three treatment plates; each plate contains four target Z. tritici colonies. Metadata therefore has 20 plate rows, while the measurement table has 80 colony rows. This example illustrates one experimental design; users should record the actual numbers of independent plates and matching controls in their own experiments.

Matching set / source folder Control image suffix Three treatment image suffixes
A33_1_14_days 28 29, 31, 32
A60_2_14_days 41 38, 39, 40
B20_2_14_days 45 42, 43, 44
B22_2_14_days 47 48, 49, 50
B37_1_14_days 33 34, 36, 37

Case-study filenames follow 2026_10_02_99_<suffix>.JPG. The generic analysis functions accept arbitrary image names. The bundled treatment codes and assignments are provisional; folder names record provenance rather than confirmed biological identity. The control’s replicate label is 1; the three treatment plates are labelled 1–3. This does not pair treatment replicate 1 only to control replicate 1: all three use that set’s single control as their denominator.

# Run the bundled measured-data example without downloading photographs:
source(system.file("examples", "04_14_day_case_study.R", package="FunMel"))

# Copy the case-study metadata to inspect its plate-level structure:
file.copy(system.file("examples", "metadata_14_day_case_study.csv",
                      package="FunMel"), "case_study_metadata.csv", overwrite=FALSE)

The example prints plate means and exports a provisional real-data comparison. Measurements were obtained from plate-image analysis. Experimental assignments, segmentation masks and calibration remain subject to review. The example demonstrates the workflow without marking these review decisions complete. The archive case-study script can also process the original photographs.

The coefficient is mean(MI_T1, MI_T2, MI_T3) / MI_control within each set. A single control supports this descriptive calculation. Inferential assessment has additional replication requirements, described below. Each independent control plate should be recorded once in the metadata.

Additional beginner examples 

source(system.file("examples", "01_image_quickstart.R", package="FunMel"))
source(system.file("examples", "02_coefficient_arithmetic.R", package="FunMel"))
source(system.file("examples", "03_fungal_matched_experiment.R", package="FunMel"))

These additional examples use synthetic data to explain masks, exact arithmetic and a replicated-control model. Scripts write to temporary output directories and print their locations. These simulated outputs demonstrate methods and are not experimental results.

3. Analyze one real photograph and inspect its mask 

img <- file.choose()
r <- analyze_plate(img, layout=plate_layout(centre="fungus"),
                   dish_diameter_mm=90, keep_images=TRUE)
plot_qc(r)
r$colonies[, c("colony_id", "detected", "MI_mean", "area_mm2")]
r$warnings

Use centre="fungus" for fungal confrontation plates and centre="none" for control plates containing only the four target colonies. Enter the actual outer dish diameter, not an assumed 90 mm. MI is mean 100 - L* on the retained colony interior: greater MI means a darker image, not a measured melanin concentration. keep_images=TRUE enables later QC plotting; batch runs save QC files and omit large image arrays from their returned object.

Photograph plates using comparable exposure, illumination and geometry. Include a suitable colour reference where possible. Inspect dish fit/scale, each target mask, central-partner assignment and candidate halo. Flat-field correction does not prove that different photographs are biologically comparable. Halo candidates are colour zones, not independently validated inhibition boundaries.

4. Prepare metadata: one row per independent plate 

make_metadata("photos", recursive=TRUE)
# Edit photos/plate_metadata.csv before analysis.

The template keeps relative source paths but leaves experimental fields for you to fill. Folder names are provenance, not sufficient evidence of treatment or control identity. A ZIP needs your metadata too: the package cannot infer the experimental design just by unzipping it. Image basenames must be unique.

Column What to enter
file Unique image basename, including extension
relative_file Relative path from the image root; useful for nested folders
plate_id Globally unique independent biological plate ID
set_id Matching control set; often an experimental batch
treatment Exact control label, or consistent treatment name
centre_model Primary assay recipes: none for controls; fungus for fungal confrontation
partner_type Biological partner type, consistent with the recipe
zymo_strain, day, medium Recommended context; if included, complete and constant within a set
metadata_confirmed Logical TRUE only after checking experimental assignments
qc_pass Logical TRUE only after acceptable mask/calibration review; required by finalization
replicate Optional plate replicate label; not the colony number
rotation_deg, radius_frac, radius_mm, search_frac Optional numeric, per-image layout settings

All treatment replicates in set S use only controls in S. Several treatments may share S’s controls: list each control plate once. The same treatment label in several sets must represent the same intervention. Give different strains, days or media separate set IDs. Four colonies on one dish are subsamples, not four independent plates. Multiple photos of one dish do not create biological replication.

The bundled inst/examples/metadata_14_day_case_study.csv illustrates this structure. For a new experiment, generate and complete a metadata template using the actual plate IDs, treatments and control assignments.

5. Analyze a folder or a ZIP 

meta <- read.csv("photos/plate_metadata.csv", stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
files <- file.path("photos", meta$relative_file)
# Alternatively, with an arbitrary original photo ZIP:
# files <- prepare_photo_archive("my_photos.zip", meta, "extracted_photos")
validate_metadata(meta, files)
out <- analyze_plates(files, metadata=meta,
                      layout=function(row) layout_by_treatment(row),
                      qc_dir="FunMel_results/qc")
saveRDS(out, "FunMel_results/image_analysis.rds")
out$failed
out$coefficient_error

For a complete generic workflow, copy and configure scripts/analyse_experiment.R. It takes any valid metadata and image paths; it does not assume particular filenames, treatment codes or replicate counts. It stops at the review stage unless both confirmation flags are TRUE. The 14-day archive script is a separately named case study, not the general entry point.

After inspecting and, where necessary, correcting the photographs/masks, update your metadata CSV. Do not set flags TRUE merely to obtain a coefficient.

reviewed_meta <- read.csv("photos/plate_metadata.csv", stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
reviewed <- finalize_analysis(out, reviewed_meta)
reviewed$melanization_coefficient
reviewed$assessment$status
reviewed$assessment$treatment_comparisons

Finalization reuses saved measurements. Changing the central segmentation recipe or an image’s layout settings requires image reanalysis; reassigning verified matching-set/treatment labels can be applied to saved measurements. Resolve failed images explicitly; do not silently drop a failed replicate.

6. Understand the coefficient and statistical assessment

For each plate, average its target colonies’ MI_mean. The matched coefficient is the treatment’s mean plate MI divided by its own set’s control mean plate MI. Plates get equal descriptive weight. MC > 1 means darker treatment images; MC < 1 means lighter images. Each treatment replicate’s ratio is also exported. Across several sets, the final descriptive coefficient averages matched set ratios equally; it does not divide by pooled unrelated controls.

assess_experiment() retains raw colony MI and fits a fixed mean for each observed set-treatment cell plus a plate random intercept: MI ~ 0 + set_treatment_cell + (1 | plate_id). lme4 fits the model and lmerTest supplies Satterthwaite contrast inference. Within-set effects are treatment - own control; treatment comparisons subtract these matched effects. Shared-control covariance is preserved. An explicit method="plate_means" alternative retains one row per independent plate and the same matched contrasts. Neither method tests treatment averages as if they were replicates.

This cell-specific model conditions on observed sets. It differs from an additive treatment + batch model or a random-batch population model. Different set coverage can confound a treatment-only interpretation; prefer comparison_scope="common_sets" where the design supports common batches. Do not feed ratios sharing one denominator to an ordinary independent-sample test.

The current implementation requires at least two independent plates in every set-treatment cell before inference; this is a conservative computational guard, not a universal assay rule or an assurance of sufficient power. A single control can support a descriptive ratio. Some sparse designs can support inference under other justified models; those must be specified separately. Singular fits or convergence issues withhold inferential tables. Inspect status, residuals and replication. Holm-adjusted p values are separate from unadjusted contrast-wise CIs.

7. Save results and a comparison figure 

write.csv(reviewed$colonies, "FunMel_results/colonies.csv", row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(reviewed$melanization_coefficient,
          "FunMel_results/matched_coefficients.csv", row.names=FALSE)
saveRDS(reviewed, "FunMel_results/reviewed_analysis.rds")
plot_treatment_comparison(reviewed,
                         file="FunMel_results/treatment_comparison")

PDF/SVG are vector exports; PNG is 600 dpi. Panel A shows plate MI and matching controls; panel B shows matched plate ratios and group ratios of means. The Outlined squares distinguish controls from filled treatment circles. Treatments use contrasting colours. Lower diamonds and bars show treatment means ± one between-plate SD; row annotations give means, SDs and plate counts. Control SD is unavailable when n=1. Ratio SD measures treatment spread conditional on its shared control, without accounting for denominator uncertainty. A companion _statistics.csv records all plotted summaries and descriptive ΔMI. Access this table without exporting using attr(p, "FunMel_statistics"), where p is the returned plot. No p-values or confidence intervals are implied. Customize labels with labels=c(fungus_A="Fungal partner A"). preview=TRUE labels an unconfirmed mapping as provisional; it does not confirm metadata or override a failed QC review. Save sessionInfo() alongside your analysis.

Output Interpretation
colonies One row per target colony; MI, shape, geometry and detection status
profiles Within-colony edge-to-centre rings, not biological replicates
plates Dish scale, central partner, halo candidate and image diagnostics
failed Image errors that require action
melanization_coefficient Set-specific descriptive ratios and plate counts
per_plate_coefficients Replicate ratios using the matching control mean
assessment Model, contrasts, replication and diagnostic status

radial_asymmetry_pct is the clear alias of legacy growth_inhibition_pct: both measure toward/away radial asymmetry, not (control growth - treatment growth) / control growth * 100. Image-derived growth inhibition requires a consistent growth measurement and its own control comparison. Spatial bootstrap intervals describe uncertainty within an image, not independent-plate variation.

8. Adapt layouts and resolve common problems 

lay <- plate_layout(centre="fungus", rotation_deg=15, radius_frac=0.5)
# For a different inoculation pattern, supply positions explicitly:
pos <- data.frame(id=c("N", "E", "S", "W"),
                  x_rel=c(0,0.5,0,-0.5), y_rel=c(-0.5,0,0.5,0))
lay <- plate_layout(centre="fungus", positions=pos)
Problem Action
Function missing / unused argument Check the loaded version and args(); restart after upgrades
Missing image Check filenames/relative paths; use the original ZIP, not the review ZIP
Four regions, wrong boundaries Inspect QC; adjust layout, imaging or supervised training
Undetected target / missing MI Correct segmentation; documented na_action="omit" is explicit, not automatic
Empty coefficient table Read coefficient_error / status; verify metadata and QC
Brightness warnings Inspect correction limits and residual agar variation; consider a colour reference or rephotography
Unresolved halo Do not replace an unresolved biological boundary with zero inhibition
Inference withheld Check independent plate counts and model diagnostics; never duplicate controls

The supported use case is a roughly circular dish with a known inoculation layout. A crowded plate, merged organisms, unknown layouts or severe reflections can require training or manual analysis. Changing layouts is supported; accuracy for every photograph is not guaranteed. The simulator tests computation under known schematic conditions, not unrestricted biological generalization.

9. Why use FunMel alongside ImageJ?

FunMel connects assay-specific image processing to explicit control metadata, repeatable batch measurements, plate-aware statistics and figure exports in one R workflow. ImageJ/Fiji already supports measurements, ROI management and macro batch processing; FunMel is not claimed to be inherently more accurate or always faster. ImageJ can remain useful for manual mask review and difficult images. See the separate, README-ready overview and algorithms.
